Overall This feels like a luxurious treatment when my skin needs extra hydration before a special occasion or after a long week. While I wouldn’t use it every day because of the price, I’d happily repurchase it as part of a weekly skincare routine. The instructions for this hydrogel mask are incredibly clear, making the application process completely straightforward. On clean-shaven skin, like my girlfriend's face, the mask fits flawlessly with absolutely zero gaps. It hugs the contours of the face perfectly. Just keep in mind that this is a deep-treatment mask. It took about 3 to 4 hours to completely dry down, turn translucent, and absorb fully into the skin. The main challenge comes if you have a trimmed beard or facial hair. The hydrogel material cannot grip hair, so the lower half of the mask will not stick properly and tends to fall off. Only the upper section secured well to my forehead and upper cheeks.However, we found some great creative workarounds so nothing went to waste! My girlfriend applied the remaining jaw and chin section to my neck 😂, which worked beautifully. We also used the tiny punch-out eye and mouth patches creatively, placing the extra pieces above my eyebrows and using the mouth cutout across the bridge of my nose for targeted hydration. Pros:Truly delivers a noticeable boost in skin hydration and plumpness. Leaves the skin feeling incredibly smooth, refreshed, and deeply nourished. High-quality ingredients that genuinely work, offering great value for money. Cons: Not beard-friendly, as the lower half slides off facial hair. Requires 3–4 hours to dry, so it is best used when you have plenty of time or as an overnight mask. Final Verdict:If you have a smooth, clean-shaven face, this mask is an easy 5-star product because the fit and skin benefits are flawless. If you have a beard, the lower half simply won't stick. However, because it is highly effective and versatile enough to be repurposed on your neck and nose, it still deserves a solid 4 stars. Highly recommended, but beard wearers beware! For the £23 I bought it for I'd say this is definitely not the worst investment I've ever made, and it absolutely does give me a far better tooth clean than any manual brush ever could. From that perspective it absolutely does what I bought it for. That being said though, I think I have to echo a lot of what other people have been saying about it, from the point of view of its downsides. I havent had quite the egregious battery life other people seem to have been experiencing, but I'd also hesitate to call the battery life "good". I live by myself, and I manage to get anywhere from two to three days out of it before it needs charging again. Its not absolutely terrible and I bought it knowing the battery life was a weak point, but if you have a full family thats using it then the battery won't last very long at all. This is a problem, considering that there's no way to know when the battery is getting low other than just how strong the motor feels when you're using it. Looking at the instructions, it seems like other models have an LED on them, but this one doesnt even have a single one. This both means that its hard to get an exact idea of when the battery needs charging, and also means you wont know when exactly its done charging either (I think maybe some people are experiencing poor battery life because they arent leaving it on for long enough, precisely because of that). You sort of just have to guess at when it might be done or check how strong the motor feels. Dont get me wrong, I like that its simple and I dont think its inherently a bad product - I intend to keep it an use it even with its flaws, just because it does everything I need it to, only really cost the equivalent of a few packets of toothburshes, and having the integrated timer is really useful. However I feel like they made it a little too simple for its own good. Not having even a single LED on there does kind of harm the functionality, given that the battery life isnt exactly stellar to begin with. I'm ok with that on balance since I'm the only one using it here, but it may well be worth it to most people to move slightly further up the like to a slightly higer end brush. I feel like its also worth noting, while we're on the subject, that the brush's charger only has a shaver plug connector, and it doesnt include an adapter for a standard wall socket. Do not use this product… - if you have ever had a bad reaction to any of the ingredients. If this applies to you, get advice from a doctor or pharmacist without using Nizoral anti-dandruff shampoo. If you are pregnant or breast-feeding - you can use Nizoral anti-dandruff shampoo if you are pregnant, think you might be pregnant or are breast-feeding. Special warnings about this product - this medicine contains 24% w/w sodium laurilsulfate in each application. Sodium laurilsulfate may cause local skin reactions (such as stinging or burning sensation) or increase skin reactions caused by other products when applied on the same area. - as with most shampoos, if any gets into your eyes bathe them gently with water. - if you have been regularly using a lotion or cream, which contains a steroid (such as betamethasone or hydrocortisone) to control your dandruff, gradually use it less over 2 - 3 weeks as you start to use Nizoral anti-dandruff shampoo. This will stop your condition flaring up while Nizoral anti-dandruff shampoo starts to work. If you have any questions about stopping your steroid lotion or cream, speak to your doctor or pharmacist. If anyone accidentally swallows this product if anyone accidentally swallows Nizoral anti-dandruff shampoo, contact a doctor or your nearest accident & emergency department (casualty) taking this leaflet and pack with you. Possible side-effects Nizoral anti-dandruff shampoo can have side-effects like all medicines, although these don't affect everyone and are usually mild. If you experience any of the following, stop using the medicine and talk to your doctor: - severe allergic reactions including swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat uncommon side-effects (less than 1 in 100 people) which may occur include: - application site reactions including itching, irritation, blistering, red, dry or tender skin or a skin burning sensation - inflamed hair follicles, hair loss or changes in hair texture - increased tear production - skin rash and dry skin rare side-effects (less than 1 in 1000 people) which may occur include: - a change in the way some things taste - eye irritation - acne - skin inflammation (dermatitis) - flaking skin - application site reactions including blistering and over-sensitivity (allergic) reactions - general allergic reaction (over sensitivity) other side effects which occur but it is unknown how often: - hair discolouration and hives, which is known as nettle rash or urticaria reporting of side-effects if you get any side-effects, talk to your doctor, pharmacist or nurse. This includes any possible side-effects not listed in this leaflet. You can also report side-effects directly via the yellow card scheme at: www.mhra.gov.uk/yellowcard by reporting side-effects you can help provide more information on the safety of this medicine. I have been using the Shark FlexStyle Multistyler for several weeks now, and I can honestly say it has completely changed my hair styling routine. The first thing that impressed me was how lightweight and easy it is to use. I have fairly long hair, and traditional hair dryers and styling tools often leave my arms tired by the time I'm finished. The Shark FlexStyle feels comfortable to hold and the rotating design makes it incredibly versatile. The Auto-Wrap Curlers were the feature I was most excited about, and they did not disappoint. I was a little skeptical at first because I've struggled with curling my own hair using conventional curling wands. However, the FlexStyle automatically wraps sections of hair around the barrel using airflow, making the process surprisingly simple. After a few attempts, I was able to create beautiful, bouncy curls that looked like I had just come from a salon. The curls lasted most of the day, especially when I used a light styling spray. The Oval Brush attachment is another standout feature. It gives my hair a smooth, voluminous blowout look without needing to juggle a separate brush and hair dryer. My hair tends to become frizzy, particularly in humid weather, but this attachment helped create a sleek finish with noticeable volume at the roots. I also appreciated the Concentrator attachment for everyday drying. It directs airflow precisely where it's needed and helps achieve a polished look much faster than my previous hair dryer. One of the biggest advantages of the Shark FlexStyle is its promise of no heat damage. As someone who styles her hair several times a week, this was a major selling point. My hair feels noticeably softer and healthier compared to when I regularly used high-heat styling tools. The intelligent temperature control gives me peace of mind that I'm not exposing my hair to excessive heat. Another positive is the speed. Drying and styling my hair now takes significantly less time than before. What used to take nearly an hour can often be done in around 20 to 30 minutes, depending on the style I'm aiming for. There is a slight learning curve with the Auto-Wrap Curlers, especially if you've never used this type of styling technology before. The attachments can also take up a bit of storage space. However, once you become familiar with the different tools, the entire process becomes very intuitive. The build quality feels premium, and the attachments connect securely. It genuinely feels like a high-end styling system designed to replace multiple separate tools. Overall, I am extremely pleased with the Shark FlexStyle Multistyler. It combines a hair dryer, curling tool, volumizer, and smoothing brush into one versatile device while being gentle on the hair. For anyone looking to achieve salon-quality results at home without excessive heat damage, I believe it is well worth the investment. It has saved me time, simplified my routine, and helped me achieve styles that I previously found difficult to create on my own. " Read more View Image Gallery Amazon Customer 5.0 out of 5 stars Images in this review Reviews with images See all photos Previous slide Next slide All photos Amazon Customer 5 out of 5 stars Cost-Per-Hour Test Results & Unboxing Video Review After 8 Weeks of Use: Proaller Heated Electric Throw 160x130 cm I bought this recently based on the good reviews and reasonable price. I already have an electric blanket for the bed, and a couple of heat pads for myself and family (you can read my reviews for these by clicking on my account name above), and wanted to try something to use more casually for the chilly days ahead. It arrived vacuum-packed with an instruction booklet, and the cable/controller/mains plug already attached, ready to use. The fabric is 100% polyester on both sides, as confirmed on the sewn-in label. The coloured side is a velvety microfleece (often sold as “flannel”), while the white side that looks like wool is “sherpa” fleece, a knitted pile that mimics sheepskin. Flannel and sherpa are style names describing the texture, not the fibre, so neither side is actual wool, but polyester. However, both sides are incredibly soft, luxuriant, and warm even as a simple blanket when unheated. I measured the cable at just over 8 feet/ 2.5m in length overall, with the controller fixed along it about 2 feet from the blanket. It is connected by a small plastic unit bonded to one corner of the blanket. With the throw laid lengthways from chest to feet, with the white fleece side down, that connector will sit either by your right shoulder or by your left foot, depending on which way up you place it. If you want the controller within easy reach, you will probably choose the corner near your right shoulder. This can matter if your nearest mains socket is on the left, as the lead may then have to run across your chest or around your back, so it is worth bearing in mind. The controller is kept sensibly straightforward with just three buttons: • On/Off • Timer • Heat Some other brands try to add in special features with more buttons, which unnecessarily complicates things without actually giving any real benefits, especially if the person using it is not tech savvy or may have poor memory. The On/Off button is slightly concave, so it can be differentiated from the other two by touch, which is helpful in the dark, or for anyone with limited vision. The plastic screen over the display is slightly frosted, being clear enough to see the numbers, but reducing reflections, which is a good little detail. Once plugged into the mains, press the power button first. The display flashes for 10 seconds. If you do nothing, it switches itself off, so press either the temperature or timer button within that time to keep it on. On start-up, the default settings appear: temperature (red) 4 and timer (green) 3. The temperature runs from 1 to 9 and then H, so effectively H = 10, which is the warmest. The timer runs from 1 to 9, each number representing hours until auto-off. Each press increases the value and then cycles back to 1; you can adjust either setting at any time. After a change, the display flashes for about 5 seconds, then holds steady, and after another 5 seconds, it dims to roughly half brightness until you press a button again. This is good, as bright LEDs can sometimes be too harsh in a dark room. The green timer number counts down by one each hour to show the remaining time. There is no “Permanent On” option for safety reasons, but you can change or reset it whenever you like. If you switch off but leave the unit plugged in, your last settings are remembered for next time. If you unplug it, the settings revert to the defaults (temperature 4, timer 3) on the next start-up. Okay, now the interesting and important part: the actual cost of running it. Although the label states 150 W, that is the maximum “draw” when the element is on. In practice, most heated throws regulate warmth by cycling on and off, so the average power over an hour is usually much lower, particularly on the mid and low settings and will vary with room temperature etc. While this brand does not publish per-setting wattages or confirm the control method, this is how products of this type generally work, so I put it to the test. I have a plug-in power meter to measure the consumption of electrical devices, and sure enough it switches between 150 W to zero every few seconds, on and off. I ran a few tests on it at different heat settings and logged wattage / energy used over 60 minutes, and therefore the actual wattage and cost. Results (Per Hour): Heat No. _Watts __ Cost 1 _______ 29w___ 0.80p 3 _______ 35w___ 0.97p 5 _______ 46w ___ 1.27p 7 _______ 63w ___ 1.74p 10 (H) ___ 79w ___ 2.18p So, on medium (5) it costs just over 1 pence per hour in electricity, and on maximum heat 10 (H) a shade over 2p per hour. These figures are based on my energy provider and area, which is currently (at the time of writing, Oct 2025) 27.72p/kWh. Yours may vary slightly (you can check on your provider’s website), but roughly it means having the throw on a high setting for five hours in the evening will cost me about 11p, and on low about 4p. When switched on, the heat feels somewhere between a heat-pad and a standard electric blanket, but closer to the latter. On level 1 it is a touch above room temperature; at the maximum, H (used instead of 10 because the display only shows a single character), it is comfortably warm and sometimes too warm, but do not expect hot water bottle type temperatures. As with electric heated pads and blankets in general, it feels warmer where it is in contact with you. Sections that hang loosely at the sides lose more heat to the air and feel cooler than areas resting directly on the body. This can seem like an inconsistency at first, but it’s really just how heat behaves, so I took a photo with a thermal camera gadget I have (see attached picture), and the heating elements seem fairly consistent in temperature across the blanket. It is washable either by hand or machine. The instructions need to be read first, as this requires removing the cable. The plug which connects to the plastic socket, fixed to the blanket’s corner, has a button on either side which need to be squeezed then pulled apart. This needs some strength and wiggling as it’s a tight fit. It goes back in one way only, and is much easier to reconnect than pull apart. All good so far. -Pros: • Low power consumption, energy saving • Ultra soft material • Simple controller • Long cable • Hand and machine washable -Cons: • Connector needs some force to detach • Not suitable to lie or sit on Overall, this is pretty much what I was hoping for, and I don’t have any real criticisms. It’s soft, warm and cosy, and I’m definitely glad I bought it now that we’re heading towards winter. I’ve already avoided putting the living room fire on at times when I normally would, as this is enough when the room is just chilly. It makes me wonder how long it will be before it pays for itself, and then possibly moves into “credit” with heating bill savings? I would definitely recommend this to anyone looking for a new option to keep warm, and as a cosy treat for yourself or a loved one, so it’s five stars from me. However, both sides are incredibly soft, luxuriant, and warm even as a simple blanket when unheated. I measured the cable at just over 8 feet/ 2.5m in length overall, with the controller fixed along it about 2 feet from the blanket. It is connected by a small plastic unit bonded to one corner of the blanket. With the throw laid lengthways from chest to feet, with the white fleece side down, that connector will sit either by your right shoulder or by your left foot, depending on which way up you place it. If you want the controller within easy reach, you will probably choose the corner near your right shoulder. This can matter if your nearest mains socket is on the left, as the lead may then have to run across your chest or around your back, so it is worth bearing in mind. The controller is kept sensibly straightforward with just three buttons: • On/Off • Timer • Heat Some other brands try to add in special features with more buttons, which unnecessarily complicates things without actually giving any real benefits, especially if the person using it is not tech savvy or may have poor memory. The On/Off button is slightly concave, so it can be differentiated from the other two by touch, which is helpful in the dark, or for anyone with limited vision. The plastic screen over the display is slightly frosted, being clear enough to see the numbers, but reducing reflections, which is a good little detail. Once plugged into the mains, press the power button first. The display flashes for 10 seconds. If you do nothing, it switches itself off, so press either the temperature or timer button within that time to keep it on. On start-up, the default settings appear: temperature (red) 4 and timer (green) 3. The temperature runs from 1 to 9 and then H, so effectively H = 10, which is the warmest. The timer runs from 1 to 9, each number representing hours until auto-off. Each press increases the value and then cycles back to 1; you can adjust either setting at any time. After a change, the display flashes for about 5 seconds, then holds steady, and after another 5 seconds, it dims to roughly half brightness until you press a button again. This is good, as bright LEDs can sometimes be too harsh in a dark room. The green timer number counts down by one each hour to show the remaining time. There is no “Permanent On” option for safety reasons, but you can change or reset it whenever you like. If you switch off but leave the unit plugged in, your last settings are remembered for next time. If you unplug it, the settings revert to the defaults (temperature 4, timer 3) on the next start-up. Okay, now the interesting and important part: the actual cost of running it. Although the label states 150 W, that is the maximum “draw” when the element is on. In practice, most heated throws regulate warmth by cycling on and off, so the average power over an hour is usually much low

Full content visible, double tap to read brief content. I bought this two-pack because I wanted to upgrade from a basic electric toothbrush, and I’m really pleased with it so far. The difference is noticeable straight away. My teeth feel much cleaner after brushing, and the iO2 is surprisingly quiet compared with other electric toothbrushes I’ve used. I really like having the pressure sensor because it’s easy to accidentally brush too hard, and the different intensity settings mean I can adjust it depending on how my teeth and gums feel. The handles are comfortable to hold and the battery life has been good, so I’m not constantly having to charge them. Getting two handles, two brush heads and the travel cases makes this feel like a much better deal than buying a single toothbrush. The black and forest green colours also look much better than the usual plain toothbrushes. The only thing I’d mention is to rinse the brush and handle properly after use, as toothpaste can build up around the head and smaller areas. Overall, I’m very happy with the purchase. It feels like a genuine upgrade from a standard electric toothbrush and I’d definitely recommend the iO2, particularly if you can get the two-pack at a good price. In the event of the CO alarm sounding, follow these 3 steps: VENTILATE : Keep calm; open doors and windows to ventilate your home. Stop using fuel-burning appliances and turn them off. EVACUATE : Evacuate the property immediately. RING FOR HELP: If in the UK, call The National Gas Emergency Service on 0800 111 999. If outside the UK, call your supplier's emergency number. Do not use appliances until they have been checked by an expert. Get medical help for anyone suffering the effects of CO poisoning. What are the symptoms of CO poisoning? Symptoms of CO poisoning include headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea and vomiting, rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath, seizures, chest pain, disorientation, and loss of consciousness. Who should I call in the event of a CO leak? If in the UK, call The National Gas Emergency Service on 0800 111 999. If outside the UK, call your supplier's emergency number. What are the sources of CO? The common sources of Carbon Monoxide (CO) are cookers, fires, boilers, oil and gas boilers, portable generators, oil or solid fuel cookers, gas or paraffin heaters, barbecues (BBQs), clogged chimneys, wood or gas fireplaces, cigarette smoke or any fossil fuel‑burning appliances.
